question: I'm thinking of letting my holiday home, and sometimes my own home, to short-stay guests through a booking site. Can I register for GST?
gold: Yes, if letting it is a taxable activity. Short-stay accommodation is a taxable supply, not the exempt supply of accommodation in a 'dwelling' (GST Act s 14(1)(c)): a 'dwelling' must be the guest's principal place of residence, where they have quiet enjoyment (s 2), and short-stay guests have neither. Registration needs a taxable activity: an activity carried on continuously or regularly that supplies accommodation for payment (s 6(1)(a)); occasional or one-off lets may not qualify. You must register if your supplies exceed $60,000 in 12 months, or are expected to (s 51(1)); below that you may register voluntarily (s 51(3)). Registering brings ongoing duties (records, returns, adjustments for private use), and GST is usually payable on the property when you deregister (s 5(3)) or sell it, unless you claimed no input tax on it, didn't buy or use it mainly for taxable supplies, and elect to keep it out of your taxable activity (s 6(3)(e)). Since 1 April 2024, bookings through an online platform such as Airbnb are 'listed services' (s 8C): the platform accounts for the GST, passing a flat-rate credit to a host who isn't registered, and a registered host's supply to the platform is zero-rated.

accept: Says short-stay guests don't occupy the home as their principal place of residence, or lack quiet enjoyment, so the exemption for accommodation in a dwelling doesn't apply.

question: Can depreciation determinations the Commissioner issued under the Income Tax Act 1994 still be used today, given that Act has been repealed and they were never reissued?
gold: Yes. A determination made under the 1994 Act that hasn't been revoked, replaced or reached its own expiry date still applies without being reissued. When the 1994 Act was repealed from 1 April 2005 (replaced by the Income Tax Act 2004, and later the Income Tax Act 2007), section 21 of the Interpretation Act 1999 kept anything done under a power in the repealed Act in effect as if done under the law that replaced it. The Interpretation Act was itself repealed on 28 October 2021; the same rule is now section 35 of the Legislation Act 2019, and s 32 keeps the earlier effect. The powers that replaced 1994 Act ss EG 4, EG 10 and EG 11 are in the Tax Administration Act 1994: s 91AAF (economic rates), ss 91AAG to 91AAJ (special and provisional rates) and s 91AAL (maximum pooling value). So the old determinations operate as if made under those sections. References in them to the 1994 Act are read as references to the matching provisions of today's Act (ITA 2007 s ZA 3(2), formerly ITA 2004 s YA 3(2)). The Commissioner can revoke a determination (e.g. s 91AAF(6)).

question: The Crown gives Treaty of Waitangi claimant groups funding towards their costs of negotiating a settlement (rent, travel, advisers' fees, hui costs and so on). If a claimant group is registered for GST, is this claimant funding subject to GST?
gold: In practice, no: Inland Revenue's published view (2006 item, still current) is that claimant funding is not subject to GST, but the law isn't settled. The claimant group supplies nothing to the Crown by negotiating a settlement, so the funding isn't 'consideration' (GST Act s 2(1)) for a supply. Nor is it 'a payment in the nature of a grant or subsidy' that s 5(6D) deems to be consideration, because the Crown pays it to meet its obligations for Treaty breaches, not as gratuitous help. Advances of financial redress used for negotiation costs are financial redress and likewise not subject to GST. Against that, s 5(6D) is wide: it covers any grant or subsidy paid on behalf of the Crown to a person 'in relation to or in respect of' that person's taxable activity, and funding for a registered group's costs could be argued to fall within it. No court has decided the point, so the 'no GST' answer rests on the Commissioner's view; a group that follows it is unlikely to be challenged by Inland Revenue. Section 5(6D) still reads the same, and the new schedule 2 list (2025) doesn't change the result.

question: I'm checking when people's KiwiSaver member tax credit eligibility started, under the definition of 'creditable membership' in section YA 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007. What is Inland Revenue's view on these three points? (1) When does 'membership' in paragraph (a) of the definition start? (2) Does that view change anything for members who joined KiwiSaver through a provider between 1 July and 30 September 2007 and made a contribution before 1 November 2007? (3) For members who joined through a provider in that same period but made their first contribution on or after 1 November 2007, when does their eligibility for the member tax credit start?
gold: (1) Inland Revenue's view is that 'membership' in paragraph (a) starts at the earlier of the provider opening an account for the member (in anticipation of allotting securities) or securities first being allotted. Automatically enrolled members are unaffected: their creditable membership starts under paragraph (b)(i), from the first day of the month in which a contribution is first deducted. Members who join directly through a provider are generally eligible from when the provider opens their account, not from when money is first transferred. (2) No change for 1 July to 30 September 2007 joiners who contributed before 1 November 2007: they fall under paragraph (b)(iii), so eligibility starts from the earlier of the first of the month in which the provider received a valid membership application, or the first of the month in which their first contribution was received by the provider or Inland Revenue. (3) If their first contribution came on or after 1 November 2007, (b)(iii) doesn't apply; eligibility starts from the earlier of the actual day the provider opened their account, or the first of the month in which their first contribution was received by the provider or Inland Revenue. The definition (Income Tax Act 2007 s YA 1) is unchanged today.

question: Before the 2011–12 income year I gave Inland Revenue a written election to treat my commercial building (estimated useful life of 50 years or more) as not depreciable property, so I have never claimed depreciation on it. Depreciation on commercial buildings was later reinstated from the 2020–21 income year, at 2% diminishing value or 1.5% straight line. What does my election mean for me?
gold: Your election still binds you. An election under ITA s EE 8 that property not be depreciable has effect for the year it is made and all later years until the building is disposed of or another event in s EE 47 occurs (s EE 8(5)); it can't be revoked to take advantage of a rate change. So you could not claim depreciation for the 2020–21 to 2023–24 income years, when commercial buildings had a 2% DV / 1.5% SL rate. From the 2024–25 income year the rate for any building with an estimated useful life of 50 years or more is 0% again (s EE 31(2)(d), (3)(c), as amended by the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Act 2024 s 55), so today the election makes no practical difference to your deductions. For other owners (QB 21/11): owners who claimed depreciation had to keep claiming at the set rate; owners who never claimed and never made a written election may still elect retrospectively (s EE 8(3)), with effect from when they acquired the building (s EE 8(6)). Inland Revenue's view is that the election must be in writing.

question: We run a New Zealand airport. Our international airline customers pay us for rubbish removal, lighting and security, parking their aircraft, and use of the terminal. Do we charge GST on those services at the zero rate?
gold: It depends on the aircraft. None of the four services is zero-rated as international transport: GST Act s 11A(1)(a) zero-rates only services that 'are the transport of passengers or goods' and excludes ancillary transport activities, and rubbish removal, lighting and security, aircraft parking and terminal services don't carry anyone or anything. But since 30 March 2025 s 11A(1)(iba) zero-rates services supplied directly in connection with craft that the Customs and Excise Regulations 1996 exempt from entry, which include an aircraft not owned or registered in New Zealand that is visiting temporarily on a commercial international voyage (reg 25(1)(b), (ba)); Inland Revenue's commentary on the 2025 Act says the paragraph covers such aircraft. So for an aircraft owned or registered in New Zealand all four services are standard-rated at 15%. For a qualifying foreign aircraft, test each service: parking the aircraft, and likely removing its rubbish, are supplied in connection with the aircraft itself and can be zero-rated; use of the terminal serves the airline and its passengers and stays at 15%; lighting and security depend on what is lit or guarded. Inland Revenue's 2022 item (QB 22/05) says all four are standard-rated, but it predates s 11A(1)(iba) and treats commercial aircraft as outside the temporary-import rule; Inland Revenue has guidance on supplies to visiting craft in its work programme, and no court has applied the new paragraph.

question: Overseas hunters' trophies from hunts in New Zealand are mounted by a New Zealand taxidermist before being exported to the hunters, which usually takes many months. For the supply to stay zero-rated, can Inland Revenue extend the 28-day export period by more than 183 days?
gold: Yes. Under GST Act s 11(5), on the supplier's application, the Commissioner may extend the 28-day period for exporting zero-rated goods where, because of the nature of the supply, export within 28 days isn't practicable (or circumstances beyond the supplier's and customer's control prevent it). The Act sets no maximum, and the old 183-day limit from a 1997 Inland Revenue item no longer applies. Inland Revenue's current guidance is IS 20/02 (May 2020), which replaced the 2007 item (QB 07/04). It accepts that trophies (souvenir animal parts or hunting souvenirs) generally can't practicably be exported within 28 days, so it grants extensions on application, for a period that suits the case, and can grant one extension covering future supplies. The exporter-supplier, normally the outfitter, applies (a taxidermist only as the outfitter's agent), before the 28 days end, with documents such as the supply contract and the time expected for the taxidermy and export. Anyone relying on an extension granted before IS 20/02 should re-apply. The 2007 item's 'generally 12 months' practice isn't repeated in IS 20/02.

question: I filed my income tax return for a year that included a particular transaction, and only afterwards applied to Inland Revenue for a private binding ruling on that transaction for the same year. Section 91E(4)(f) of the Tax Administration Act 1994 says the Commissioner may not make a private ruling once an assessment has been made for the person, the arrangement and the year, unless the application was received first. Does my own return, as a self-assessment, count as that assessment?
gold: Yes. Under TAA s 91E(4)(f) the Commissioner may not make a private ruling if an assessment relating to the person, the arrangement and a period or tax year the ruling would cover has been made, unless the application is received before the date the assessment is made. 'Assessment' is defined in s 3 to include an assessment of tax made under a tax law by a taxpayer or by the Commissioner, so it covers a self-assessment. Since self-assessment began (2002–03 income year), a taxpayer who must file a return has to assess their own taxable income and tax (s 92(1)), and that assessment is made on the date the return is received by Inland Revenue (s 92(2)); for an individual it is treated as made when their account for the year is finalised, which is when they file (ss 92(2B), 22I(2)). So once your return reached Inland Revenue before your ruling application, s 91E(4)(f) bars a private ruling on that transaction for that year. The policy reason is that a transaction already covered by an assessment should be dealt with through the disputes process instead. A ruling is still possible for years not yet assessed.

question: Inland Revenue issued me a private ruling that contains a small error. The error can't be fixed under section 91GI of the Tax Administration Act 1994, it isn't material, and Inland Revenue and I agree it doesn't change the ruling's conclusion but should still be corrected. Can the Commissioner withdraw the ruling and issue a corrected replacement ruling that applies back over all or part of the same period?
gold: In practice, yes: Inland Revenue's published view (QB 08/02) is that the Commissioner can do this, but the law isn't settled. Sections 91E(4)(e) and 91F(4)(e) of the Tax Administration Act 1994 bar a new private (or product) ruling only if a ruling 'already exists' for the same person, arrangement and period. Inland Revenue's view (QB 08/02) is that this test is applied when the replacement is issued, and once the original has been withdrawn (by notice under s 91EI(1)) it no longer exists, so the Commissioner can issue an amended replacement ruling for some or all of the same period. That reading fits the purpose of the rulings regime, which is to give taxpayers certainty. The other reading: s 91EI(3)(b) says a withdrawn ruling 'continues to apply' to an arrangement entered into before the withdrawal, so it could be said still to exist for that period, which would bar a replacement for it. Inland Revenue itself accepts the point is unclear, and no court has decided it. The practical risk is small: on the other reading the original ruling, whose conclusion is the same, would still apply for that period. A 2008 transitional limit for rulings issued under the Income Tax Act 2004 no longer matters in practice.

points.says: Reaches a reasoned conclusion on whether the bar on a new ruling where one already exists stops a replacement ruling for the same period, either way: it doesn't, because a withdrawn ruling no longer 'exists' when the replacement is issued; or it does, because a withdrawn ruling still applies to earlier arrangements and so still exists for that period.
points.quote: a private ruling already exists on how the relevant taxation law applies to the person and the arrangement

points.quote: the ruling continues to apply, for the remainder of the period or tax year specified in the ruling, if the arrangement was entered into before the date of withdrawal

topic: Tax administration: binding rulings and double tax agreements
question: Can Inland Revenue give a private or product ruling on an issue that is already covered by a mutual agreement made by the competent authorities under a double tax agreement?
gold: No. The Commissioner can make binding rulings only on how a 'taxation law' applies (TAA ss 91B, 91C(1), 91E(1), 91F(1)). A mutual agreement between competent authorities is not a taxation law, so the Commissioner has no power to rule on what a mutual agreement means or how it applies. In addition, ss 91E(4)(d)(ii) and 91F(4)(d) bar a private or product ruling on a matter that is being dealt with, or in the Commissioner's opinion should be dealt with, by one or both competent authorities under a double tax agreement. Inland Revenue's view (QB 08/03) is that an issue within the scope of an existing mutual agreement should continue to be dealt with by the competent authority, so it will not rule on it. A matter is 'being dealt with' where the taxpayer has presented a case under the treaty's mutual agreement procedure, or the competent authorities are negotiating a wider agreement on it. The taxpayer should take the issue to the competent authority instead.

points.says: Concludes no: Inland Revenue won't give a private or product ruling on an issue within the scope of an existing mutual agreement.
points.quote: the matter on which the ruling is sought is being dealt with, or in the Commissioner’s opinion should be dealt with, by one or both competent authorities of the parties to a double tax agreement
points.cite: Tax Administration Act 1994 s 91F(4)(d) (product rulings); s 91E(4)(d)(ii) (private rulings, same words)

points.says: Names TAA s 91E (private rulings) or s 91F (product rulings) as the source of the bar on a ruling on a matter being dealt with, or that should be dealt with, by the competent authorities under a double tax agreement.
points.quote: is being dealt with, or in the Commissioner’s opinion should be dealt with, by one or both competent authorities of the parties to a double tax agreement

points.quote: A mutual agreement is not a "taxation law" as defined in section 91B of the TAA, as it is not a provision in any of the statutes specified in section 91C(1) of the TAA.

question: In the 2008–09 income year, a company in our group carries out research and development, but another group company funds the work and bears its financial risk. So on its own the R&D company can't claim the R&D tax credit, because it doesn't fully meet the requirements in section LH 3(1) of the Income Tax Act 2007, although the group as a whole does. We plan to restructure so that the R&D company funds the work itself and bears its financial risk; it has the staff and capital to manage that risk and will genuinely incur all the expenditure. Is that tax avoidance under section BG 1?

Getting the R&D credits is clearly a purpose or effect of the restructure: before it, the company couldn't meet s LH 3(1) on its own (performing or having the R&D performed, controlling it, bearing its financial risk, effectively owning its results, and incurring the eligible expenditure). But Parliament enacted the credit to encourage investment in R&D. After the restructure the company bears the costs and financial risk that Parliament intended a claimant to bear, so its claim is consistent with Parliament's purpose, and the restructure involves no pretence or artificiality. Parliament would not have meant to deny the credit in these circumstances. This answer is for 2008–09: the subpart LH credit was repealed from 1 April 2009, and today's R&D tax incentive (subpart LY) has different rules. Section BG 1 itself (a tax avoidance arrangement is void against the Commissioner) is unchanged.

question: Our iwi's Treaty of Waitangi deed of settlement has the Crown pay, on top of the agreed financial and commercial redress, an extra amount calculated on that redress for the period from signing the deed until the redress is paid. The deed calls this amount 'interest'. Is this settlement interest taxable income?
gold: No. Settlement interest is a capital receipt and not taxable income: that is Inland Revenue's published view (QB 09/01), and its later item on time-value payments (QB 22/01) says it doesn't contradict it, and replaces it only on how s CA 1(2) works with the specific income provisions. Inland Revenue's September 2026 commentary on the 2026-27 Bill still cites QB 09/01. It isn't income under the financial arrangements rules, because a Treaty settlement is not a financial arrangement (ITA s EW 3): the Crown pays to compensate past losses, not in return for anything provided to the Crown, and a settlement that depends on legislation involves no debt. It isn't 'interest' under the statutory definition (s YA 1), because the claimants haven't lent money or given credit to the Crown, so s CC 4(1) doesn't apply. That doesn't end the question: a payment that compensates for the time value of money can still be income under ordinary concepts (s CA 1(2)) if it has the characteristics of income, and its label or the way it is calculated doesn't decide its character. Settlement interest lacks those characteristics. It keeps the agreed redress at its value during the delay before settlement legislation is passed, so it is part of the price of securing the settlement and a further instalment of compensation for a capital loss, like the redress itself. This assumes the usual deed, where the settlement is conditional on settlement legislation. It rests on the Commissioner's published view; no court has decided the point.

question: I own a holiday house in New Zealand. My family uses it over summer and on some weekends, and I rent it out to other people from time to time. How is it taxed?
gold: For the 2026–27 income year, rent you receive is taxable income (ITA s CC 1). How costs are treated depends mainly on whether the house sits unused for at least 62 days in the year. A typical holiday home that does is a 'mixed-use asset' (s DG 3: land used partly to earn income and partly privately, and not in use for at least 62 days). Then costs that relate only to renting (such as advertising) are fully deductible and purely private costs are not (s DG 7); shared costs such as rates, insurance, interest, repairs and depreciation are deducted by the formula expenditure × income-earning days ÷ (income-earning days + private-use days) (s DG 9), so empty days count for neither. Private use includes use by you, family and other associates, and letting at less than 80% of market rent (s DG 4). If gross rent is under $4,000 you can choose to treat it as exempt and claim nothing (s DG 21); if it is under 2% of the property's rateable value or cost, a loss is quarantined (s DG 16). Residential rental loss ring-fencing doesn't apply to it (s EL 12). If the house is unused for fewer than 62 days, these rules don't apply: costs are deductible only to the extent they are incurred in earning the rent, not private (ss DA 1, DA 2(2)).

topic: Income tax: 'common law interest' and ordinary income
question: Some read the High Court's decision in CIR v Buis (2005) as holding that 'common law interest' (interest-like payments not connected with lending, such as late-settlement interest under a contract or interest awarded with damages) can't be taxed as income under ordinary concepts under section CA 1(2) of the Income Tax Act 2007, because it falls outside the statutory definition of 'interest'. Does Inland Revenue accept that as a general principle?
gold: No. Inland Revenue's current view is in QB 22/01 (April 2022), which replaced QB 09/03. A payment that compensates for the time value of money but falls outside the statutory definition of 'interest' (ITA s YA 1) can still be taxable: under s CA 1(2) as income under ordinary concepts if it has the character of income, or under another provision. Calling it 'interest' doesn't decide this either way. The YA 1 definition is exhaustive, so such a payment can't be taxed as interest under s CC 4(1). On Buis itself, Inland Revenue now reads the judgment as consistent with its view: it doesn't stand for a broader rule that such payments can never be income, and its outcome is confined to the particular ACC penalty payments in that case. The 2009 position (QB 09/03), that the Commissioner didn't accept that part of Buis as a general principle and intended to have it tested in court again, has been replaced.

topic: International: NRWT on interest to an Australian lender
question: I live in New Zealand and own one rental house in Melbourne, which I bought with a loan from an Australian bank. An Australian property management company, which manages properties for many owners, looks after it for me. Do I have to pay New Zealand non-resident withholding tax on the interest I pay the bank?
gold: It depends on the bank. Under the law for the 2026–27 income year, interest on money lent outside New Zealand to a New Zealand resident has a New Zealand source (ITA s YD 4(11)(b)(i)), so interest paid to a non-resident lender is non-resident passive income subject to NRWT (s RF 2(1)(a)(iv)), which you as payer must withhold. Two exceptions. (1) If the lender is a registered bank doing business in New Zealand through a fixed establishment (branch) here and isn't associated with you, the interest is excluded from NRWT (s RF 2(2B)(b)). (2) There's no New Zealand source if the money is used for a business you carry on through a fixed establishment outside New Zealand; but one rental house is generally not a 'substantial business', so you have no fixed establishment in Australia, even with an Australian manager (Inland Revenue QB 09/05). So if the bank has no New Zealand branch, NRWT applies, and the New Zealand–Australia tax treaty caps it at 10% of the gross interest (art 11(2)); interest an unrelated bank derives would be exempt (art 11(3)(b)), but not where the payer hasn't paid approved issuer levy (art 11(4)(a)). Alternatively you can elect to pay approved issuer levy (TAA s 32M): register the loan, pay a 2% levy (Stamp and Cheque Duties Act s 86J), and NRWT on the interest falls to 0% if you and the bank aren't associated (ITA s RF 12).

topic: GST: change-in-use adjustment for land (pre-2011 rules)
question: As at 1 March 2010: I'm GST-registered and bought a block of bare land for the main purpose of making taxable supplies, claiming input tax on the purchase. I've since set aside part of the land for a non-taxable use (a family house), which is a deemed supply under section 21(1)(a) of the GST Act. How do I apportion the land's cost to work out the cost of that part under section 10(8)(a)?
gold: Inland Revenue's view (QB 09/06, 2009) is that apportioning the land's cost pro rata by area will generally be appropriate. Under s 21(1)(a) as it stood on 1 March 2010 you are treated as supplying the part applied to a non-taxable use, and s 10(8) values that deemed supply at the lesser of its cost to you (including the input tax claimed) and its open market value. The 'cost' of the part is its share of the original purchase price. A pro rata split isn't appropriate where it isn't realistic to give every part the same share of the cost: for example where the block has areas with markedly different features (flat pasture against beach or lake frontage, or swamp), parts zoned differently, a right of way or easement over part, or a sale agreement that allocates the price. Then another method can be used, such as splitting the price by the parts' relative market values at the time of purchase. Any method must be intelligible, based on the facts known when the land was bought (not its later use), and not too theoretical or artificial (Lowe v CIR (1981); CIR v Walker [1963]). These rules were replaced for supplies made on or after 1 April 2011.

accept: Says any reasonable method based on facts known at purchase can be used, and that splitting by area is appropriate where the parts of the land are of similar character or value.
points.quote: The Commissioner considers that a pro rata method of apportionment of cost for the purposes of section 10(8)(a) will generally be appropriate for deemed supplies of bare land under section 21(1)(a).

question: What is the GST treatment of providing or assigning futures contracts that are cash-settled, that provide for physical delivery of a commodity whose supply is exempt from GST, or that provide for delivery of money?
gold: No GST is charged in any of the three cases. Providing or assigning a futures contract, through a defined market or at arm's length, is a 'financial service' under GST Act s 3(1)(k) where the contract (i) doesn't provide for delivery of a commodity (a cash-settled contract), (ii) provides for delivery of a commodity whose supply is exempt, or (iii) provides for delivery of money (or, since a 2022 amendment backdated to 2009, cryptocurrency). A supply of financial services is exempt (s 14(1)(a)). If the supply would be zero-rated under s 11A, zero-rating takes priority over the exemption (s 14(1B)(a)): Inland Revenue's view (QB 10/02) is that a cash-settled futures contract supplied to a non-resident who is outside New Zealand when the contract is entered into is zero-rated under s 11A(1)(k). question: For fringe benefit tax, when does the fact that a car the employer now owns was previously owned by the employer, or by a person associated with the employer, change the value used to work out the FBT?
gold: FBT on a car the employer owns is based on either the car's cost price to the employer or its tax value (ITA Schedule 5 clause 1(a)). Normally the starting point is the employer's actual cost (tax value is that cost less depreciation). Earlier ownership matters if, in the 2 years before the employer most recently acquired the car, the car was owned by the employer or by a person associated with the employer. Then, on the cost price basis, the cost price is treated as the highest cost price paid for the car by the employer or an associate since it was made (clause 8(b)); on the tax value basis, the tax value is worked out under clause 4, using a deemed cost set by clauses 5 to 7 (for example the highest cost on any acquisition, or the earlier owner's tax value if higher). Inland Revenue's view (QB 10/03): the 2 years run back from the employer's latest acquisition, not from when the car is first provided to an employee; the parties must have been associated at some time in that period while the associate owned the car; and the rule applies even if an unrelated owner held the car in between. These are anti-avoidance rules against selling and buying back a car to lower its FBT value.
